1.assumed: Current is the rate of flow of charge, and Kirchhoff's first law expresses conservation of charge.

2.assumed: Third force for equilibrium equals the resultant of the other two (Pythagoras) but opposite in direction.

3.assumed: Acceleration starts at g, decreases as drag grows with speed, reaching zero at terminal velocity.

4.assumed: Energy gained in eV adds to kinetic energy; speed scales with √(KE).

5.assumed: Period = 1/f; time-base = period ÷ number of divisions it spans.

6.assumed: Stationary-wave amplitude varies from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes; progressive wave amplitude is uniform.

7.assumed: p = √(2m·KE) from Ek = p²/2m; λ = h/p with proton mass.

8.assumed: Same wire material and area: drift velocity ∝ current; branch currents split inversely with resistance.

9.assumed: Extra weight divided by extra extension (in m) gives k.

10.assumed: Weight acts at the centre; its moment uses the perpendicular distance, falling as cos θ to zero at vertical.

11.assumed: A floating object is in equilibrium, so upthrust equals its weight.

13.assumed: Reaction time is the constant-speed section; braking distance is the area under the decelerating part.

14.assumed: At rest drag is zero; buoyancy exceeds weight so resultant and acceleration are upward.

15.assumed: Clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments about the hinge; solve for the cable distance.

16.assumed: Electric charge is measured in coulombs.

17.assumed: Work (Fx) and moment (Fd) are both force × distance, N m.

18.assumed: Fundamental in a closed tube: length is a quarter wavelength; f = v/λ.

19.assumed: A stress–strain line returning along the loading line shows elastic behaviour.

20.assumed: Ions carry current in electrolytes; conventional current flows from + to −.

21(a).assumed: In perfectly elastic collisions both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.

21(b).assumed: Total momentum starts at zero, so the person gains equal and opposite momentum, moving slower as heavier.

22(a).assumed: Rearrange k = F/v² and use N = kg m s⁻².

22(b).assumed: Percentage uncertainties add; a squared term doubles; convert to absolute and give 2 s.f.

23(a)(i).assumed: Resultant joins tail of the first vector to head of the second in a tip-to-tail diagram.

23(a)(ii).assumed: Use the cosine rule or measure a scale drawing.

23(b)(i).assumed: Stress = F/A, strain = stress/E, extension = strain × length.

23(b)(ii).assumed: Gradient of v–t gives acceleration; upward acceleration needs tension above weight, deceleration below.

24(a)(i).assumed: A non-zero intercept indicates a systematic error such as lead or contact resistance or a zero error.

24(a)(ii).assumed: Gradient of R against L is ρ/A; measure diameter with a micrometer; A = πd²/4.

24(b)(i).assumed: Convert kW to W and divide total power by power per mat.

25(a).assumed: Internal resistance adds to total resistance, reducing current; some e.m.f. is lost as lost volts.

25(b).assumed: Series lamp carries total current; parallel lamps share it equally at the same p.d.; read values from the graph.

26(a).assumed: Coherent waves have a constant phase difference.

26(b).assumed: Read period from graph; f = 1/T with ms converted.

26(c).assumed: Intensity ∝ amplitude²; ratio of intensities is the squared amplitude ratio.

26(d).assumed: Resultant displacement is the sum of individual displacements at that instant.

27(a).assumed: Superposition: resultant displacement equals the vector sum of individual displacements.

27(b).assumed: Maxima from constructive interference (path difference nλ), minima from destructive ((n + ½)λ).

27(c).assumed: Fringe spacing = speed × time between maxima; λ = ax/D.

28(a).assumed: One photon releases one electron; KEmax = hc/λ − φ; zero at threshold wavelength.

28(b)(i).assumed: E = hc/λ with nm converted to m.

28(b)(ii).assumed: Photons per second = power (mW to W) ÷ photon energy.
